extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in journalism/media studies; journalists and newsroom managers interested in the sociology of news production
extracted.subtask_description: Describes how newsroom organizations assess and classify occurrences as news, including the temporal and spatial routines, typifications (hard/soft/spot/developing/continuing), resource constraints, and technology that shape what becomes news. Useful for understanding and evaluating news selection processes in daily newspapers and broadcast newsrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness as a negotiated phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: The assessment of newsworthiness is a negotiated phenomenon, constituted in the activities of a complex bureaucracy designed to oversee the news net.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors continually create and recreate negotiated standards of judgment; selection reflects organizational routines and bureaucratic editorial hierarchy. Inclusion/exclusion is shaped by institutional centralization, who produced an item (reporter, stringer, staff or AP), and overlapping responsibilities. Example: wire services and major newspapers mutually accommodate national vs international emphasis. Anti-pattern: treating newsworthiness as an independently derived objective criterion rather than a product of organizational negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchoring newsworthiness in space (spatial news net)
rubrics_metrics.description: The news net is anchored in space: occurrences are expected to occur at specific locations, and reporters concentrate in central spatial locations to find potential news events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial conferences, bureaus, and the geographic dispersion of reporters structure which events are noticed and covered. Examples: City Hall bureaus keeping track of reporters; London bureau editing copy so New York editors have material ready. Implication: proximity and presence at key places increase the chance an occurrence will be considered news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchoring newsworthiness in time (temporal rhythm)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rhythm of newswork — reporters' office hours, skeleton night staffs, deadlines — objectifies time and shapes which occurrences can be covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most reporters attend between ~10:00–11:00 A.M. and leave 6:00–7:00 P.M.; skeleton staffs and 'lobster shift' cover late editions. Temporal synchronization with source office hours (e.g., City Hall) affects coverage. Consequence: occurrences outside concentrated hours require exceptional merit to get coverage (e.g., evening events must be a 'damned good story').

rubrics_metrics.name: Typifications (use of categories to reduce idiosyncrasy)
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations must reduce idiosyncratic occurrences to known classifications (typifications) so they can process the glut of potential stories; typifications are embedded in practical, time-linked tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typifications (as distinct from abstract categories) are grounded in routinized work and help plan and allocate resources. Analogies used: hospitals reducing patients to symptom sets; typifications routinize events so organizations can anticipate and act. Anti-pattern: attempting to process each occurrence as wholly unique would be organizationally impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard news versus soft news distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard news concerns occurrences potentially available to analysis or interpretation and typically consists of factual presentations; soft news (features/human-interest) concerns the texture of human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard-news prototypes: gubernatorial message, State of the Union, accidents, murders, legislative proposals. Soft-news prototypes: human-interest items (cheerful bus driver, lonely bear). Hard news tends to be timely/important to citizens; soft news is less time-sensitive and can be prepared in advance (e.g., Sunday features, 'Man in the News'). Overlap exists and the same event can be treated as hard or soft by different outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spot news (unscheduled, immediate events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spot news refers to unscheduled, unforeseen events that appear suddenly and must be processed quickly (e.g., fires, robberies, accidents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot news requires rapid allocation of resources and often round-the-clock staffing to anticipate rare but critical events (e.g., presidential coverage). Processing is constrained by distance, deadlines, and available personnel. Technology and deadlines (film development for TV, print deadlines) shape response options (overtime, pulling reporters/cameramen, hiring freelancers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Developing news (facts emerging over time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing news is a subclass of hard news characterized by evolving information: a story remains 'developing' while relevant 'facts' are still emerging and being gathered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished from spot news by the amount and evolution of available information rather than subject matter. Developing stories demand ongoing resource allocation as new facts arrive; technology and newsroom rhythms affect how quickly facts can be gathered and disseminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing news (series over time, prescheduled or protracted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuing news comprises a series of stories on the same subject occurring over a period (e.g., legislative bills, trials, campaigns, wars) and often involves prediction and planning about future developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuing stories are often prescheduled or follow predictable institutional processes; they require planning across days and may lead to assigning reporters to cover long trials or campaigns exclusively. Newsrooms anticipate resource drains and may free assigned reporters from other duties for the duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling types and their impact (nonscheduled, prescheduled, unscheduled)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events-as-news are classified by scheduling: nonscheduled (timing determined by newsroom), prescheduled (announced future date), and unscheduled (unexpected occurrence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most hard news is prescheduled or unscheduled; nonscheduled hard news (investigative stories) can be held for later dissemination (e.g., Pentagon Papers). Soft news is more often under newsroom control (nonscheduled/prescheduled) and can be prepared in advance. Scheduling affects when facts are gathered and how resources are allocated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / 'quickening' (perishability of news)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quickening' (speed) is the essence of news; hard-news stories become obsolete quickly while soft-news is less time-sensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworkers distinguish stories by how rapidly they become outdated; failure to act quickly renders a hard-news story useless. This drives rush to publish/broadcast, affects editorial decisions, and interacts with technology and staffing constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource availability and allocation constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of reporters, editors, and technical staff across time influences which occurrences are covered and how; finite personnel/time means many potential stories cannot be processed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reserve reporters held for emergencies; assigning a reporter to a long trial removes them from daily beat coverage; late-evening occurrences require special competitive merits to displace scheduled material. Newsrooms triage stories (writing obituaries, rewrites, or handling press releases) to conserve capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology shapes news typifications and processing
rubrics_metrics.description: The technologies used (print vs film/video vs live remote) have distinct time rhythms and resource demands that influence typifications and how events are covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television can shoot/edit/air faster than print, but film development and editing create deadlines (e.g., need footage by 4:00 P.M. to air at 6:00 P.M.). Print is more labor-intensive; television may lack reserve crews and must choose among costly responses (overtime, freelancers). Technology choices condition newsroom allocation strategies and what stories are feasibly covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification depends on mode of occurrence as much as content
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworkers' classifications are 'relatively content free' — typifications draw on the way occurrences happen (timing, predictability) not solely on subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., fires tend to be spot news because they occur unexpectedly; legislative bills are continuing because they unfold over time. Thus the manner of occurrence (scheduled/unscheduled, predictable rhythm) often drives classification and resource planning.
